analysis.one_liner: Repeals all Clean Air Act protections for the ozone layer.
analysis.headline: A single-sentence bill to wipe out federal ozone-layer protections died in committee with 4 cosponsors and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Tom DeLay's bill would have deleted Title VI of the Clean Air Act in its entirety — the federal program that phases out chemicals like CFCs and halons that destroy the ozone layer [S3] [S2]. The ozone program was created to prevent a thinning ozone layer from raising rates of skin cancer, cataracts, and other harm from ultraviolet radiation. The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee, then to its Health and Environment subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever took place before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that produced or depended on ozone-depleting chemicals would have gained: makers of CFCs and halons, pest-control and structural fumigation companies that relied on fumigants restricted by the phaseout, refrigeration and aerosol users facing retrofit costs, and growers using methyl bromide. Repeal would have erased federal phaseout deadlines and spared them the cost of switching to substitutes [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users and makers of ozone-depleting chemicals

how_it_helps.text: It would have repealed Title VI of the Clean Air Act outright, eliminating the federal schedule for phasing out production and use of chemicals that destroy stratospheric ozone, such as CFCs and halons [S3] [S2].

Industries that still depended on those chemicals — including fumigation and pest control, refrigeration, and agriculture's use of methyl bromide — would have avoided the cost and disruption of the mandated switch to substitutes, because the legal requirement to switch would no longer exist [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The general public. The ozone phaseout is the mechanism credited with allowing the ozone layer to recover, and undoing it would have left no federal program limiting ozone-depleting chemicals, with the resulting ultraviolet exposure falling on everyone — elevated skin cancer and cataract risk over decades. Businesses that had already invested in CFC-free technology would also have been undercut by laggards [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The public's health, via UV exposure

drawbacks.text: Repeal would have eliminated the entire federal ozone-protection program with nothing to replace it, abandoning the US commitments built around the Montreal Protocol and undoing a phaseout already well underway, which would slow the ozone layer's recovery and raise long-term skin cancer risk for the public [S2] [S3].

Companies that had already spent money converting to ozone-safe chemicals would have faced competitors free to keep using cheaper banned substances — meaning the bill would have penalized compliance while rewarding delay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a one-sentence repeal of an entire statutory title, offering no transition plan, no substitute program, and no accounting for the public-health stakes [S3]. Its only real benefit was short-term cost relief for a narrow set of chemical users, and even that was questionable, since the international Montreal Protocol treaty and market conversion to substitutes were already in motion. The costs — slower ozone recovery, decades of added cancer and cataract risk, and punishment of businesses that had already complied — far outweighed anything the bill offered.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tom DeLay introduced the bill on January 11, 1995, as a single section repealing Title VI of the Clean Air Act, the stratospheric ozone protection program [S1] [S3].
Four House Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no Democrats did [S4].

The House referred the bill to the Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced, and on February 6, 1995 it was referred onward to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment — the last action ever taken [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public came out ahead: the ozone phaseout stayed on the books and the recovery of the ozone layer continued. Businesses that had already invested in ozone-safe substitutes were also spared unfair competition from laggards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; ozone protections stayed on the books

for.name: Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal all Clean Air Act ozone-protection provisions

for.name: Four House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health and Environment subcommittee and never reported it out; no hearing or markup was ever held

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll call to measure the split; the bill's only recorded support was a Republican sponsor and four Republican cosponsors, with no Democratic cosponsors.

industries.industry: Ozone-depleting chemical producers (CFC and halon manufacturers)
industries.note: The bill would have repealed the phaseout of their core products, extending sales of chemicals scheduled to be banned. Their gain would have come directly at the public's expense through higher ultraviolet exposure.
Fumigation depended on chemicals subject to the ozone phaseout, so repeal would have removed the mandate to switch to alternatives. The public would have borne the health cost of continued emissions.

Growers faced the scheduled phaseout of methyl bromide, a potent ozone-depleting fumigant; repeal would have extended its availability. The savings for a few crops would have been paid for in public health.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of ozone-safe substitutes and retrofitted equipment
industries.note: These companies had invested in compliance with the phaseout, and repeal would have let competitors keep using cheaper banned chemicals, undermining their investments.
